items.title: 68357_Jimmy Maxwell oral history interview
items.q: The interviewer lists Jelly Roll Morton among 'greats' like Louis Armstrong and Charlie Shavers who have passed away, noting that young musicians may not know about them. The interviewee does not provide any personal anecdote or confirmation of a direct relationship in this segment.

ctx.x: And I just happened to mention I have difficulty sometimes describing to young black musicians who don't know too much about their background, the younger ones nowadays, in the

seventies, doesn't seem too much interested. And I made the statement that now that so many of our greats have passed like Louis Armstrong and Charlie Shavers and Jelly Roll Morton and any number of greats, Jimmy Blanton, that many young blacks don't really know anything about them or even be too interested in learning.
And you made a statement to me about what you thought when you have run into that. Please, go on now.

items.title: 68357_Jimmy Maxwell oral history interview
items.q: Interviewer mentions 'great black composers, like Jelly Roll' and Interviewee responds generally about teachers and pupils without referencing Jelly Roll personally.

ctx.x: Oh, yeah, I do believe it, yes. I do believe that. And I like Trumbauer myself. That's one of the few musicians from that circle -- I never liked Bix Beiderbecke. I never understood what the hollering was all about. And the funny thing, the first person that made me see any value at all, was Lloyd Reese, a black trumpet player. And he said, don't put him down just because he doesn't sound like Louis Armstrong. He said, there's a lot to learn from him. And he pointed it out but at that time I couldn't see it. Now,…

Yet, to take the opposite side of what you say of events, I agree with you on events, the young black player, perhaps, he might be crowded. But now that we have schools and quite a number of our young black musicians are in school, and we have jazz workshops, we have some people -- we're beginning to get into that. But I find that some of our regular -- some of our popular black stars are not -- don't go back and do a Louis Armstrong song in 1979. I happen to remember hearing some black instrumentalist that had…

anything on Shades of Louis, some name players. You know, I don't want to throw anyone's name in particular, but I was wondering -- and yet we have some white players that have been doing some excellent jobs on recreating and reviving and bringing a rebirth to some of our great black composers, like Jelly Roll and some of great pianists. We know who they are. And I don't remember, recently, any of our name black artists doing this kind of thing. I was wondering what you think about that?
